ev.ind_fc_nakshatra.shanti.ok: Three brahmins chanted over the fire, pouring ghee into the flames, and your father, they say, slept soundly for the first time in a week. The chart, marked with a note of the rite performed, went into the chest.
ev.ind_fc_nakshatra.syllable: Name by the star, without the rite
ev.ind_fc_nakshatra.syllable.ok: You were named on the syllable your nakshatra required, and there they left it. Your father keeps his spirits up, but at festivals he now and then gives you a sidelong look.
ev.ind_fc_nakshatra.ignore.ok: Your father heard him out, thanked him and forgot it. "The gods did not give me a child in order to take it back," he said.
ev.ind_fc_nakshatra.title: Birth star
ev.ind_fc_nakshatra.text: Your father touched your lips with honey and ghee, then sent for the astrologer. The jyotishi spent a long time drawing your chart and frowned: you were born under the nakshatra Mula, "the root" — such a child, they say, brings misfortune on its father. The brahmins can turn it aside with a pacifying rite, a shanti, and it costs a good deal. Or you can simply be named on the syllable the star prescribes, and trust the gods.
ev.ind_fc_nakshatra.note: Hindu birth rites included jatakarma (honey and ghee on the baby's lips) and namakarana, the naming on the 10th–12th day. The first syllable of the name was often chosen by the nakshatra, the lunar mansion of birth. Birth under Mula was thought dangerous for the father — and, in a bride, for her father-in-law — and a Mula-shanti rite was performed for protection. Charts were later compared when marriages were arranged.
ev.ind_fc_nakshatra_match.title: The charts agree
ev.ind_fc_nakshatra_match.text: Matchmakers came, and their astrologer compared your chart with theirs most carefully. Seeing Mula, he raised his eyebrows — but beside it was the note of the shanti performed, and he nodded: "The obstacle is removed." The matchmakers left content, and for the first time your household spoke of a wedding in earnest.
ev.ind_fc_nakshatra_doubt.title: The match falls through
ev.ind_fc_nakshatra_doubt.text: The matchmakers were already at the door when their astrologer found Mula in your chart. "Such a child brings misfortune on the house it marries into," he said, and the matchmakers left with apologies. Now the house is silent, and your father is looking for a brahmin to perform the shanti even at this late hour.
ev.ind_fc_nazar.kajal: A black dot and a thread
ev.ind_fc_nazar.kajal.ok: Grandmother painted a fat dot of kajal — soot mixed with oil — on your cheek and tied a black thread round your wrist. By morning you were asleep, from the dot or from sheer exhaustion.
ev.ind_fc_nazar.dargah: Carry you to the saint's tomb
ev.ind_fc_nazar.dargah.ok: The saint's tomb smelled of roses and incense. A keeper passed a peacock-feather fan over you, and your mother tied a red thread to the lattice of a window — with a prayer.
ev.ind_fc_nazar.healer.ok: The healer felt your belly, sniffed your swaddling and prescribed fennel water. "Not the eye — colic," he said, and took his fee. By midnight you were quiet.
ev.ind_fc_nazar.title: The evil eye
ev.ind_fc_nazar.text: The guests vied in praising how pretty and chubby you are — and since evening you have screamed without stopping, and your mother is at her wits' end. The women agree: the evil eye! A black dot could be painted on your cheek, you could be carried to the dargah — the tomb of a Sufi saint, where Muslims and Hindus alike go — or a healer could be called, a vaidya or a hakim.
ev.ind_fc_nazar.note: Belief in the evil eye, nazar, was shared by the Hindus and Muslims of India; to this day children are given a black kajal dot against it. The tombs of Sufi saints, dargahs, were revered by people of both faiths: sick children were brought there and threads tied with prayers. Akbar himself went to pray for a son to Shaikh Salim Chishti, and the heir born in 1569 was named Salim.
ev.ind_fc_nazar_urs.title: The saint's urs
ev.ind_fc_nazar_urs.text: For the urs — the anniversary of the death of the saint to whose tomb you were carried as a baby — the whole district gathered. Qawwals sang until dawn, and next to you in the crowd sat someone your age of the other faith: you clapped in time and chattered as if you had known each other all your life. Since that night you have a friend.
ev.ind_fc_nazar_healer.title: The healer's shop
ev.ind_fc_nazar_healer.text: The old healer who once treated your colic recognised you at the bazaar: "The little screamer {g:himself|herself}!" He invited you into his shop to grind herbs, and over the winter you learned what fennel is good for, and what turmeric and ginger cure.
